usage: at the start of the month
Add 에 for the time point
from the beginning of the month
examples: I get my salary at the beginning of the month.
I'm usually not busy at the start of the month.
I start exercising from the beginning of the month.
nuance: 월초 means the first few days of a month, not just the 1st. Koreans often pair it with 월급(salary) and 월말(end of month) when talking about money and schedules. It sounds natural in everyday planning conversations.
mistakes: Writing 월 초 with a space (it is one word: 월초)
Confusing 월초 with 초(second) — here 초 means 'beginning'

usage: at the end of the month
Add 에 for the time point
until the end of the month
examples: I have no money at the end of the month.
I have a lot of work until the end of the month.
I meet my friend at the end of the month.
nuance: 월말 is the opposite of 월초 and refers to the last days of the month. It often comes up when talking about bills, rent, and running low on money. Pairing 월초 and 월말 together sounds very natural to Koreans.
mistakes: Writing 월 말 with a space (it is one word: 월말)
Using 끝 instead of 말 — 월말 is the fixed word for 'end of month'

examples: I give flowers on the anniversary.
nuance: 기념일 is any special day worth remembering, but Koreans especially use it for couples and weddings. Young couples often celebrate 100일(100 days) and 1주년(1 year) as 기념일. It carries a warm, celebratory feeling.
mistakes: Writing the gloss as 'memorial day' — 기념일 is broader and usually personal

usage: Add 에 for the time point
the first day of the trip
examples: It rained on the first day of the trip.
여행 첫날 is a natural pairing
I'm nervous on the first day of school.
There's a lot of work from the first day.
nuance: 첫날 is the very first day of something — a trip, a job, school, or a vacation. The 받침 of 첫 makes it sound like '천날'. It often carries a feeling of newness or nervousness.
mistakes: Writing 첫 날 with a space (it is one word: 첫날)
Saying 처음 날 — the correct form is 첫날

usage: at the end of the year
Add 에 for the time point
examples: There are many gatherings at the end of the year.
I meet my family at the end of the year.
The end of the year is always busy.
nuance: 연말 refers to December and the close of the year, a season full of gatherings and parties in Korea. The set phrase 연말연시 covers both the year-end and the new year. It carries a busy, festive feeling.
mistakes: Confusing 연말(end of year) with 월말(end of month)
Writing 연 말 with a space (it is one word: 연말)
